title: As Heat Waves Spike, the Global South Needs New Cooling Solutions
gist: Global air-conditioner demand could grow from 1.5 billion to 5.5 billion units by 2050, requiring roughly 697 TWh of new generation capacity; geothermal-powered thermal energy networks (TENs) offer up to 50% energy savings over conventional AC and are already deployed at scale in China and Europe, with the Global South's best opportunities concentrated in the Gulf, parts of Latin America, and Southeast Asia.

insights.claim: The number of air conditioners in use globally is projected to rise from 1.5 billion today to 5.5 billion by 2050 as incomes and temperatures rise, primarily in emerging markets.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Signals a multi-decade capex cycle in cooling equipment, refrigerants, and grid capacity concentrated in developing economies.
insights.quote: There are 1.5 billion air conditioners in use around the world today. By 2050, as incomes and temperatures rise, that number could hit 5.5 billion.
insights.locator: There are 1.5 billion air conditioners

insights.claim: The IEA projects that from 2025 to 2035 the global increase in electricity demand will be primarily driven by cooling demand in emerging markets and developing economies.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Utilities and power-infrastructure investors in EM should treat cooling load, not industrial or EV demand, as the dominant near-term driver of power demand growth.
insights.quote: the global increase in power demand will be primarily driven by cooling demand in emerging markets and developing economies
insights.locator: The International Energy Agency (IEA) projects

insights.claim: Meeting projected growth in global cooling demand will require adding about 697 terawatt hours of generation capacity, roughly equal to the entire current electricity generation of Brazil, the world's sixth-largest electricity producer.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of new power infrastructure investment cooling alone will demand, a useful benchmark for grid and generation capex forecasts.
insights.quote: the world will need to add 697 terawatt hours—as much generation capacity as currently exists in Brazil, the world’s sixth-largest electricity producer
insights.locator: To satisfy the growth in cooling demand

insights.claim: In New Delhi, the number of extreme heat days per year is expected to rise from 36 currently to 48 by 2050.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete regional benchmark for modeling climate-driven cooling infrastructure demand growth in South Asia.
insights.quote: the number of extreme heat days is expected to increase from the current rate of thirty-six days a year to forty-eight days a year by 2050
insights.locator: In cities like New Delhi

insights.claim: Air conditioning, combining fossil-fuel-based electricity generation and refrigerant emissions, accounted for 3.2 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2022, a share expected to keep rising with global usage.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Growing AC-related emissions increase regulatory and carbon-pricing exposure for AC and refrigerant manufacturers over time.
insights.quote: air conditioning accounted for 3.2 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2022, and this number will only increase as global usage skyrockets
insights.locator: Between fossil-fuel-based electricity generation

insights.claim: Extreme heat caused an estimated $16 trillion in global economic losses between 1992 and 2013, and U.S. productivity losses from heat exposure alone are projected to reach $500 billion by 2050.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Frames climate-adaptation cooling infrastructure as a hedge against a large and growing macro productivity drag, strengthening the investment case for cooling capex.
insights.quote: one study estimates that between 1992 to 2013, $16 trillion was lost to the effects of extreme heat
insights.locator: Extreme heat conditions also lead to economic disruptions

insights.claim: Conventional air conditioners perform worse in hot, humid climates — precisely the regions where cooling demand is growing fastest — because they must run longer and harder to remove both heat and humidity, raising electricity consumption and lowering efficiency.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Structural inefficiency of AC in tropical growth markets creates an opening for district cooling alternatives to capture share as those markets urbanize.
insights.locator: Existing air conditioners are electricity-intensive

insights.claim: The authors argue policy should not discourage individual air-conditioner adoption, since it is often life-saving for the elderly and vulnerable, but should instead introduce lower-emission alternatives like district cooling to curb load growth.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Positions district cooling as complementary to, not a replacement for, individual AC — relevant framing for companies selling either technology into the same markets.
insights.quote: The solution is not to discourage cooling devices.
insights.locator: The solution is not to discourage

insights.claim: District cooling systems, which pipe centrally chilled fluid to networked buildings, can cut energy use by up to 50 percent compared with conventional individual air conditioning.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: A roughly 50% efficiency gain creates a clear investable value proposition for real-estate developers and utilities building new dense developments.
insights.quote: in the case of district cooling, energy savings could be up to 50 percent
insights.locator: District energy requires less electricity

insights.claim: Thermal energy networks (TENs) — Generation V district energy systems with heat pumps at every connected building — are on average three times more efficient than air-source heat pumps and six times more efficient than electric baseboard heaters.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Establishes TENs as a materially more efficient technology class worth tracking for climate-tech and infrastructure capital allocation.
insights.quote: The average TEN is three times more efficient than air-source heat pumps and six times more efficient than electric baseboard heaters
insights.locator: Thermal energy networks (TENs) are decarbonized

insights.claim: A 2021 study found a typical Massachusetts household on a geothermal thermal energy network could spend up to 60 percent less annually on heating than a comparable home using a gas furnace.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: A clear cost advantage over gas heating strengthens the case for utilities to convert gas district heating infrastructure to geothermal, as Eversource has begun doing.
insights.quote: a typical Massachusetts household on a geothermal TEN could spend up to 60 percent less annually on heating compared to a similar home using a gas furnace

insights.claim: Absorption chillers can use low-grade geothermal or waste heat instead of grid electricity to cool water for building distribution, reducing reliance on electricity in cooling-constrained markets.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: An electricity-light cooling pathway is especially attractive in emerging markets with constrained grid capacity.
insights.locator: Absorption chillers, an additional technology option

insights.claim: Boreholes for district-scale geothermal systems typically only need to reach a few hundred feet deep, shallow enough for conventional drilling rigs, lowering the technical barrier to deployment relative to deep geothermal power projects, though local drilling expertise still affects costs and timelines.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Lower technical barriers than deep geothermal power suggest faster replicability across markets lacking specialized drilling capacity, easing execution risk for financiers.

insights.claim: China is currently the largest market for geothermal district energy systems, with deployments reported across roughly seventy cities in eleven provinces.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: China's early lead signals both a domestic market and a potential exporter of equipment and expertise as other emerging markets adopt the technology.
insights.quote: The largest market for geothermal district energy systems is China, where such systems can now be found in a reported seventy cities across eleven provinces.
insights.locator: The largest market for geothermal district energy

insights.claim: Germany plans to double its geothermal district heating capacity to 850 megawatts thermal by 2030, a policy push accelerated by the loss of Russian natural gas supply after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Illustrates how energy-security shocks, not just climate policy, can catalyze geothermal district energy investment — a pattern that could repeat in other gas-import-dependent markets.

insights.claim: The International Finance Corporation, part of the World Bank Group, has signed agreements to support geothermal district energy deployment in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan and Dushanbe, Tajikistan, and has solicited proposals for projects in Pakistan and Jordan.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Identifies specific frontier markets where multilateral development finance is already de-risking geothermal district energy, creating a pipeline for private co-investment.

themes.theme: Mapping Global South cooling potential to 2040

insights.claim: The authors built a country-level "TEN potential" score for 2040 by multiplying each country's projected urbanization rate by the projected number of days per year its heat index will exceed 35°C, to identify where cooling demand coincides with the building density needed for cost-effective district energy.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Provides investors a replicable, reusable framework to rank country-level district-cooling opportunity by combining climate and urbanization data.
insights.locator: TEN potential was calculated as the product

insights.claim: By 2040, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, and Qatar are projected to face daily heat index temperatures above 35°C for a third or more of the year, representing acute district-cooling demand despite already being highly urbanized.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Gulf states already investing heavily in urban megaprojects are prime near-term markets for district-cooling capital deployment.

insights.claim: The Philippines, Mexico, and Colombia combine favorable geothermal permitting regimes, identified in the authors' July 2025 paper on geothermal electricity permitting, with high projected TEN cooling potential, creating synergy between low regulatory risk and demand.

insights.so_what: These three countries stand out as lower-regulatory-risk entry points for geothermal district-cooling investment relative to peers with high demand but weak permitting.

insights.claim: The only currently operational geothermal district cooling project in the Global South is in Abu Dhabi, where ADNOC and Tabreed have added geothermal cooling, drilled by an Icelandic firm, to the G2COOL district cooling network at Masdar City, supplying about 10 percent of the development's cooling demand from two geothermal wells.

insights.so_what: A concrete, named, operating commercial precedent investors can benchmark unit economics and JV partnership structures against.

insights.claim: Many banks and project finance entities avoid funding geothermal projects because they are unfamiliar with the underlying project economics; the authors argue multilateral development banks, revolving loan funds, and sovereign wealth funds should help fill this financing gap.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: Identifies a financing bottleneck — and the institutional investor types positioned for early-mover advantage by underwriting geothermal district energy before commercial banks catch up.

insights.claim: Detailed project-level cost data for geothermal thermal energy network deployment is largely not publicly available, and the authors argue greater transparency is needed for development finance institutions and urban planners to properly assess project viability.
insights.speaker: Daevan Mangalmurti
insights.so_what: A current data-transparency gap that early movers with proprietary cost data could use as a competitive moat, or that data providers could fill as a market niche.

insights.claim: The authors identify airports, convention centers, business districts, and university campuses — rather than residential developments — as the most likely first-mover sites for district energy deployment, given lower stakeholder complexity for institutional or single-owner sites.

insights.so_what: Suggests initial commercial opportunities in geothermal district cooling will center on institutional real estate and infrastructure clients rather than residential builders.
